title: CBC Interpretation: Read the Pattern, Not One Cell Line
bottomLine: A CBC is a pattern of red cells, white cells and platelets. Interpret each abnormality with indices, differential, trend and clinical context; pancytopenia, rapidly falling counts or cytopenias with bleeding/infection are qualitatively different from one stable mild abnormal value.
recognize: Hemoglobin/hematocrit reflect oxygen-carrying red-cell mass but change with volume status; WBC/differential reflects immune-cell distribution; platelet count informs primary hemostatic risk.
Simultaneous abnormalities in multiple cell lines raise marrow, medication, severe infection, nutritional, immune or infiltrative questions.
differentiate: Microcytosis, normocytosis and macrocytosis organize anemia evaluation; neutrophilia and lymphocytosis have different differentials; thrombocytopenia is not synonymous with DIC.
A laboratory flag must be reconciled with smear quality, prior results and symptoms before it becomes a diagnosis.
assessment: Assess fatigue/dyspnea, infection/fever, bruising/bleeding, medications, alcohol, nutrition, pregnancy, recent chemotherapy, chronic disease and prior counts.
workup: Use indices, reticulocytes, smear and cause-directed iron/B12/folate, hemolysis, renal, inflammatory, infectious or marrow testing according to the pattern rather than ordering every study at once.
management: Treat the cause; escalate severe symptomatic anemia, febrile neutropenia, major bleeding with thrombocytopenia or rapidly progressive pancytopenia.
medicationSafety: Chemotherapy, immune therapies, antimicrobials and other drugs can suppress cell lines; review timing and drug-specific monitoring requirements.
counselling: Explain which cell line is abnormal and what symptom should trigger urgent reassessment rather than describing the whole CBC as simply 'bad'.
followUp: Repeat counts at a clinically meaningful interval tied to the suspected cause or treatment effect; persistent unexplained multilineage abnormalities warrant hematology assessment.
examTrap: Seeing a high WBC and diagnosing bacterial infection without the differential, symptoms or source—or calling isolated thrombocytopenia DIC.
oneLinePearl: CBC interpretation starts by asking which cell line, what pattern, and how fast it changed.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Medical Laboratory Science recommendations

title: Platelets and Coagulation: Count, Function, and Cascade Are Different
bottomLine: Platelet count, platelet function and coagulation-factor testing answer different questions. Do not order PT/aPTT as a generic bleeding screen or assume a normal coagulation panel excludes platelet dysfunction, von Willebrand disease or a clinically important anticoagulant effect.
recognize: Low platelets impair primary hemostasis; PT/INR and aPTT reflect selected coagulation pathways; neither measures platelet function.
Bleeding phenotype matters: mucocutaneous bleeding suggests platelet/vWF problems more than deep-tissue hemarthrosis patterns, though overlap exists.
differentiate: A normal PT/aPTT does not rule out von Willebrand disease or qualitative platelet dysfunction.
DOAC effect is not reliably quantified by routine PT/aPTT; warfarin is monitored with INR and UFH monitoring is assay/protocol specific.
assessment: Assess bleeding site/severity, medication/anticoagulant/antiplatelet exposure, liver disease, pregnancy, infection, prior bleeding and family history.
workup: Order platelet count, PT/INR, aPTT and specialized assays only when the clinical question warrants them; repeat critical values when specimen error is plausible but do not delay action by reflex re-draws.
management: Treat active major bleeding and the cause; reversal/transfusion decisions depend on the drug, procedure, platelet count/function and clinical severity rather than a single universal threshold.
medicationSafety: Anticoagulants and antiplatelet drugs affect different parts of hemostasis; medication reconciliation is essential before interpreting tests.
redFlags: Severe thrombocytopenia with neurologic or bleeding symptoms
counselling: Explain that a 'normal INR/PTT' does not mean every bleeding mechanism is normal.
followUp: Close the loop on abnormal coagulation studies and drug timing; unexplained recurrent bleeding may require specialized hematology testing.
examTrap: Ordering PT/aPTT as a routine preoperative screen in a low-risk asymptomatic patient or using them to declare a DOAC absent.
oneLinePearl: Hemostasis has platelets, proteins and drugs—one test never measures all three.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Using Labs Wisely

title: Calcium Disorders: Correct the Context, Treat the Symptoms
bottomLine: Interpret calcium with albumin/protein status or ionized calcium when clinically necessary, renal function, magnesium, phosphate and symptoms. Severe symptomatic hypocalcemia or hypercalcemia is an emergency; a mildly abnormal total calcium in an otherwise stable patient is a different problem.
recognize: Hypocalcemia can cause paresthesias, tetany, seizure or QT prolongation; hypercalcemia can cause dehydration, constipation, weakness, confusion, kidney injury and arrhythmia.
Hypomagnesemia can make hypocalcemia refractory because magnesium affects PTH secretion/action.
differentiate: Low total calcium from hypoalbuminemia may not equal low biologically active ionized calcium.
Hypercalcemia differential includes primary hyperparathyroidism, malignancy, medications and other endocrine/granulomatous causes.
assessment: Assess mental status, neuromuscular symptoms, ECG/rhythm, hydration, renal function, malignancy history, supplements/medications and prior calcium/PTH pattern.
workup: Confirm the abnormality appropriately and use magnesium, phosphate, PTH, renal function, vitamin D or malignancy workup according to the direction and clinical context.
management: Treat symptomatic severe hypocalcemia with monitored calcium therapy and correct magnesium; severe symptomatic hypercalcemia requires acute volume/supportive treatment and cause-specific therapy.
medicationSafety: Digoxin, QT-prolonging risk, thiazides, lithium, calcium/vitamin D products and antiresorptive therapy can change the clinical significance or treatment plan.
counselling: Explain that calcium balance depends on kidney, parathyroid, vitamin D, magnesium and medications—not dietary calcium alone.
followUp: Stable abnormalities need cause-directed follow-up; repeat calcium without investigating a persistent pattern is incomplete care.
examTrap: Giving more calcium repeatedly for refractory hypocalcemia while ignoring severe hypomagnesemia.
oneLinePearl: When calcium will not correct, check the magnesium and the physiology behind it.

title: Magnesium Disorders: Small Number, Big Electrical Consequences
bottomLine: Magnesium abnormalities matter most through neuromuscular and cardiac effects and through their interaction with potassium and calcium. Correct clinically significant magnesium deficiency when hypokalemia or hypocalcemia is refractory, and treat severe hypermagnesemia as a medication/renal-clearance emergency.
recognize: Hypomagnesemia can contribute to weakness, tremor, seizure, ventricular arrhythmia/torsades and refractory hypokalemia/hypocalcemia.
Hypermagnesemia is most concerning with renal impairment or excessive magnesium exposure and can cause hyporeflexia, hypotension, bradycardia and respiratory depression.
differentiate: Serum magnesium is an imperfect proxy for total-body stores; symptoms and associated electrolyte/ECG findings matter.
A patient with persistent low potassium despite replacement may need magnesium correction rather than simply more potassium.
assessment: Review GI losses, diuretics, PPIs, alcohol, nutrition/refeeding, renal function, magnesium-containing laxatives/antacids and ECG symptoms.
workup: Check potassium, calcium, renal function and ECG when clinically important; investigate chronic losses/exposure based on context.
management: Replace magnesium orally or IV according to severity/symptoms and local protocol; severe symptomatic hypermagnesemia requires stopping exposure, supportive care and enhanced elimination when indicated.
medicationSafety: Renal failure increases magnesium accumulation risk; IV magnesium requires appropriate monitoring and product/rate protocols.
counselling: Review OTC laxative/antacid use because hidden magnesium exposure can matter in renal impairment.
followUp: Recheck after significant replacement and address the cause of ongoing loss or accumulation.
examTrap: Escalating potassium replacement indefinitely while severe hypomagnesemia remains untreated.
oneLinePearl: Magnesium is the electrolyte that often explains why potassium and calcium refuse to behave.

title: CK and CK-MB: Muscle Injury Marker, Not the Modern MI Test
bottomLine: Total CK is useful for skeletal-muscle injury such as rhabdomyolysis; CK-MB should not be routinely paired with modern cardiac troponin for chest-pain/MI diagnosis. Use troponin plus ECG/clinical context for myocardial injury and CK plus renal/electrolyte assessment for muscle breakdown.
recognize: Marked CK elevation with muscle pain/weakness, dark urine or precipitating crush/exertion/toxin raises rhabdomyolysis concern.
CK-MB is less cardiac-specific than troponin and generally adds little to a contemporary troponin pathway.
differentiate: Troponin answers myocardial injury; CK answers muscle-cell injury; neither alone tells you the cause.
Rhabdomyolysis can cause hyperkalemia, AKI, phosphate/calcium disturbances and arrhythmia even before creatinine peaks.
assessment: Assess muscle symptoms, crush/immobility/exertion, seizures, hyperthermia, drugs/toxins, statins, renal function, urine output and ECG/electrolyte symptoms.
workup: Use total CK, creatinine, potassium and other electrolytes/urinalysis as clinically appropriate for muscle breakdown; use high-sensitivity troponin for suspected ACS rather than reflex CK-MB.
management: Treat rhabdomyolysis with cause control, fluids when appropriate and close renal/electrolyte monitoring; manage ACS through the troponin/ECG pathway.
medicationSafety: Statins, toxins and drug interactions can contribute to muscle injury; do not diagnose statin myopathy from one CK value without symptoms/context.
redFlags: Chest pain with ischemic ECG/troponin pattern
counselling: Explain why CK-MB is not a necessary 'second heart test' when a validated high-sensitivity troponin pathway is used.
followUp: Trend CK/renal/electrolytes when severe rhabdomyolysis is being treated; stop testing when it no longer changes management.
examTrap: Ordering CK-MB with every troponin because more biomarkers must be safer.
oneLinePearl: Troponin is the cardiac injury biomarker; CK is mainly a skeletal-muscle injury tool now.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada CK-MB lab stewardship resources

title: Respiratory Acidosis: Ventilation Failure Until Explained
bottomLine: Respiratory acidosis means CO2 retention from inadequate effective ventilation. Decide whether the process is acute or chronic by the pH/bicarbonate response, then find the cause—sedation, airway/lung disease, neuromuscular weakness, obesity hypoventilation or ventilatory failure—before treating the number.
recognize: High PaCO2 with acidemia supports acute respiratory acidosis; chronic hypercapnia may have compensatory bicarbonate elevation and a less acidemic pH.
A normal oxygen saturation does not guarantee adequate ventilation, especially with supplemental oxygen.
differentiate: Do not call every high bicarbonate metabolic alkalosis when chronic CO2 retention explains renal compensation.
Mixed disorders occur when the measured compensation does not fit the expected physiologic direction.
assessment: Assess mental status, respiratory rate/effort, airway, sedatives/opioids, COPD/OSA/obesity, neuromuscular weakness, chest mechanics and oxygen/ventilation support.
workup: Use ABG/VBG context, electrolytes and cause-directed imaging/toxicology/neuromuscular evaluation; trend gas results only when they change ventilation decisions.
management: Support ventilation and treat the cause; reverse specific sedative toxicity when appropriate and escalate noninvasive/invasive ventilation for worsening failure.
medicationSafety: Opioids, benzodiazepines and other sedatives can precipitate hypoventilation; oxygen alone does not fix CO2 retention.
counselling: For chronic hypercapnia, review sleep-disordered breathing, inhaler/sedative use and when worsening somnolence/dyspnea requires emergency care.
followUp: Reassess gas/clinical ventilation after intervention and ensure chronic causes receive definitive follow-up.
examTrap: Increasing oxygen repeatedly for a somnolent hypercapnic patient without addressing ventilation.
oneLinePearl: CO2 is a ventilation problem first; oxygen saturation cannot answer that question alone.

title: Respiratory Alkalosis: Why Is the Patient Hyperventilating?
bottomLine: Respiratory alkalosis is excessive effective ventilation causing low CO2. Anxiety is one cause, not the default diagnosis; hypoxemia, pulmonary embolism, sepsis, pregnancy physiology, liver disease, pain and toxicologic causes can produce the same gas pattern.
recognize: Low PaCO2 with alkalemia supports respiratory alkalosis; chronic compensation lowers bicarbonate.
Tingling/lightheadedness may occur from acute alkalemia but should not shortcut the search for the cause.
differentiate: A first episode of tachypnea/chest symptoms needs cardiopulmonary and metabolic assessment before being labelled panic.
Mixed metabolic acidosis plus respiratory alkalosis can occur in sepsis or salicylate toxicity.
assessment: Assess oxygenation, chest pain/dyspnea, fever/sepsis, pregnancy, pain, neurologic disease, liver disease, medications/toxins and panic pattern.
workup: Use ECG, imaging, cultures, lactate, pregnancy or toxicology testing according to the differential; calculate whether compensation is appropriate when a mixed disorder is suspected.
management: Treat the trigger rather than trying to normalize CO2 directly; provide emergency treatment for PE, sepsis, hypoxemia or toxicologic causes when present.
medicationSafety: Do not give sedatives solely to suppress hyperventilation before excluding dangerous causes.
counselling: When panic is established, explain the physiology without implying the symptoms were imaginary.
followUp: Persistent unexplained hypocapnia needs cause-directed evaluation rather than repeated reassurance.
examTrap: Calling respiratory alkalosis anxiety in a tachypneic patient with PE risk before checking oxygenation and the cardiopulmonary differential.
oneLinePearl: Low CO2 tells you the patient is ventilating hard; it does not tell you why.

title: Metabolic Acidosis: Calculate the Gap, Then Find the Cause
bottomLine: Metabolic acidosis means reduced bicarbonate from acid accumulation or bicarbonate loss. Use anion gap, clinical context and respiratory compensation to distinguish DKA/lactate/toxins/renal failure from diarrhea/RTA and to detect dangerous mixed disorders.
recognize: High-anion-gap acidosis commonly reflects lactate, ketones, renal failure or toxins; normal-gap acidosis suggests GI bicarbonate loss or renal tubular causes among others.
Kussmaul-type hyperventilation is compensation, not the primary respiratory disease.
differentiate: A normal pH does not exclude metabolic acidosis when a simultaneous alkalosis is present.
Failure to lower CO2 appropriately suggests added respiratory acidosis and worse ventilatory reserve.
assessment: Assess perfusion/shock, diabetes/SGLT2 use, renal function, diarrhea, toxins/alcohols/salicylates, pregnancy, infection and ventilation.
workup: Calculate anion gap and use glucose/ketones, lactate, renal/electrolyte studies and toxicology/osmolality as the differential requires; compare measured respiratory compensation to expected physiology.
management: Treat the cause—resuscitate shock, treat DKA, restore bicarbonate loss, manage renal failure or toxins—and monitor potassium/ventilation closely.
medicationSafety: Insulin shifts potassium; bicarbonate therapy is not a universal treatment for all metabolic acidosis and can create sodium/CO2/volume problems.
counselling: After recovery, teach disease-specific prevention such as diabetes sick-day rules or medication/toxin avoidance.
followUp: Trend the cause marker and acid-base resolution; in DKA, gap/ketone resolution matters more than glucose alone.
examTrap: Treating the low bicarbonate directly while missing shock, DKA, renal failure or toxin as the cause.
oneLinePearl: In metabolic acidosis, the gap narrows the cause and compensation tells you whether breathing is keeping up.
